# Climate Change Analysis 2: full workbook contents, with formulas

Converted from `Climate_Change_Analysis_2.xlsx` (workbook version 1.7.11, 2026-10-23) to
Markdown for reading by a language model. All 22 worksheets and all non-empty cells are
included, and every formula in the workbook is recorded.

## How to read this file

**Coordinates.** Each worksheet is a `## Sheet:` section, in workbook tab order, as one
Markdown table. The first table column, `row`, is the real Excel row number, and each header
cell is prefixed with its real column letter, e.g. `N: Residual`. Cross-references written
inside the workbook (`Volcanic!N39`, `Forcing!T33`, `Kernel!P62:Q70`, `Diagnostics!AR16`)
therefore resolve directly in this file. Columns that are empty across a whole sheet are
omitted, so header letters can skip (…`Q`, `S`…); row alignment is otherwise exactly as in
Excel, which matters because these sheets put a label in one column and its value a few
columns to the right. These sheets are sparse by design: a data series on the left, panels of
assumptions, regression statistics and commentary to the right, so many cells are
legitimately blank.

**Formulas.** A cell that carries a formula shows it next to its value, in the form
`0.1512988  {=AVERAGEIFS(...)}`. The exception is a formula filled down a column for hundreds
of rows: repeating it on every row would bury the file, so each such fill is listed once in
that sheet's **Formula columns** table, which gives the column, the row range, and the
formula as written in the first row of the range (row numbers in it shift down the column in
the usual way). Cells inside a listed fill show values only. So: every formula in the
workbook is here, once per fill or once per cell.

**Values.** Values are the ones Excel cached, printed to 10 significant figures, which
also clears binary-float noise (`0.08000000000000007` → `0.08`). Where a formula cell has
no cached value, the value shown comes instead from a LibreOffice recalculation of this
same file, checked cell by cell against the scripts listed in `Sources` section E.
No value in this export comes from the recalculation. Every formula cell that carries a cached value is shown with Excel's own; the 393 that carry none are blank-by-design guards, formulas such as IF(x="","",...) whose result is empty, so the recalculation is blank for them too and there is nothing to fall back to.

**The two engines.** From v1.7.4 the workbook ships as saved by Microsoft Excel 16.0300, so
the values above are Excel's own. They were reconciled against a LibreOffice recalculation
of the same file: 120,565 numeric cells, which is every computed cell in it, with no
difference beyond 1e-9 relative, and 107,465 formulas unchanged by the round trip. The
three reference tabs added in v1.7.5 are text only and change neither figure. That
reconciliation is worth
stating because the engines did once disagree. Through v1.7.2, seven formulas in
`Diagnostics` section C passed a lone boolean array to `SUMPRODUCT`, as in
`=SUMPRODUCT(($B$9:$B$822>=2016))`. LibreOffice coerces such an array to numbers; Excel does
not, so in Excel those seven returned 0 and the eighteen cells dividing by them showed
`#DIV/0!`, from v1.1 onward, while the pasted figures, all four scripts and every Markdown
export stayed numerically right. It surfaced only when the file was opened and saved in
Excel and that cache was compared against this export. v1.7.3 rewrote the seven as
`SUMPRODUCT(--(...))`; v1.7.4 is the first export in which Excel has confirmed the fix. The
lesson generalizes: a figure confirmed by one engine is unconfirmed.

**Conventions carried over from the workbook.** A value shown in blue in Excel was computed
outside the workbook and pasted; the four scripts responsible are listed in `Sources` section
E. Yellow cells are hand-maintained inputs. Blue and yellow do not survive into Markdown, so
use `Sources!B50:F55` and the assumption blocks to tell which is which.

**Indentation.** Leading spaces inside a cell are preserved, because this workbook uses them
to nest sub-items under a panel heading (`Single-regressor fits`, then `  log2(CO2): °C per
doubling`). Read a leading-space cell as a child of the nearest unindented label above it.

**Escapes.** `\|` is a literal pipe inside a cell. A line break inside a cell is shown as
` / `. The two raw NOAA CO2 tabs keep their `#` comment header, reassembled into a code block
above the data (the original comment lines contained commas, so Excel split them across
columns).

| 20 | Solar (TSI) | No trend since 1958 in the TSI record used, and R² ≈ 0.00 on its own, so the Sun cannot be the warming trend in that record (confirmed with NOAA Solar CDR v3 on the Sensitivity tab). But an 11-year cycle consistent with the published ~0.1 °C swing appears in the residuals at ~0.07 °C per W/m² of TSI (~0.40 per W/m² of forcing). Adding TSI moves the CO2 slope from 2.640 to 2.644 on the same months; the apparent drop to 2.64 from 2.73 is the shorter window, not the Sun. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 21 | ENSO (ONI) | The dominant short-term noise. Best lag 3 months, ~0.09 °C per unit ONI, both consistent with textbook values (the lag was selected on this record, so this is consistency, not independent recovery). The ONI series used has essentially zero linear trend over the sample (its 30-year base periods are re-centred), so it absorbs none of the CO2 trend here and the CO2 coefficient does not materially move. ONI is not a complete ENSO control (RONI and ERSSTv6 exist; see data note). |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 22 | Volcanic (AOD) | Best lag 6-8 months; implied peak cooling Pinatubo -0.25, Agung -0.18, El Chichón -0.13 °C. Transient response to a pulse (~0.13 °C per W/m²) is far below the sustained-forcing response (~0.40), which is why summing forcings of different duration and regressing makes the fit worse. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 23 | Response kernels | Replacing single lags with one-box exponential responses (τ ≈ 6 months for ENSO, 12 for volcanic AOD) improves the fit on identical months (R² 0.898 → 0.904) and leaves the CO2 coefficient at 2.70. τ was chosen on the full record; under blocked 7-fold cross-validation with τ and coefficients chosen out-of-fold, the same τ values are selected in nearly every fold and the pooled out-of-fold R² is 0.887 (CO2-only 0.838), so the specification is not an in-sample artefact, though the ΔR² is modestly optimistic. Filtering CO2 the same way has no R² optimum: the record cannot separate transient from equilibrium response. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 24 | Full forcing (ERF) | Anthropogenic ERF gives 0.40 °C per W/m², 1.6 °C per doubling when scaled by F2x (not TCR), inside the IPCC range. log2(CO2) and anthropogenic ERF are almost perfectly collinear (r = 0.997), so either fits equally well; this does NOT mean CO2 is a constant share of human forcing (its share falls from ~2.3× to ~0.75× of net anthropogenic ERF as aerosol offset shrinks), and the regression does not separate the components. Splitting human forcing into a warming term and an aerosol term gives the same response to each: 0.409 against 0.414 °C per W/m², a difference of -0.005 (Forcing!T21:T22). CORRECTED in v1.6: before that revision this split omitted the other anthropogenic column and reported 0.47 against 0.37, which was an omitted-variable artefact. The two series are nearly orthogonal over this record, so the regression does separate them, but because aerosol ERF is the widest uncertainty in AR6 the data fix the aerosol contribution rather than the response per W/m². See Open Items section B. Giving volcanic ERF its own coefficient gives R² 0.96 and leaves the F2x-scaled (not TCR) value at ~1.59. Aerosol ERF changes ~0.15 W/m² 2019-25 in this dataset, worth ~0.06 °C, so it explains part but not most of the 2023-25 excess. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 26 | What this analysis does and does not show |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 27 | Does: over 1959-2025, log2(CO2) and anthropogenic ERF are interchangeable regressors (r = 0.997). GISTEMP regressed on that proxy plus ONI has in-sample R² ≈ 0.89 monthly and ≈ 0.95 annual; both are dominated by the shared trend, and after linear detrending the annual r is 0.64 (R² 0.40). On matched months, adding ONI, AOD or TSI leaves the CO2 slope within ~0.02 of its CO2-only value. Blocked cross-validation with lag structure and coefficients chosen out-of-fold gives pooled R² 0.887 (Kernel!P62:Q70). Scaling the anthropogenic-ERF slope by F2x gives 1.61 °C per doubling (95% 1.34 to 1.87 with F2x uncertainty; 1.43 to 1.78 at 90% with IGCC ERF uncertainty propagated, Sensitivity!AC46), which is numerically inside the AR6 TCR likely range; that is a comparison, not a validation, since it is not the TCR estimand. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 28 | Does not: estimate equilibrium climate sensitivity (a 66-year single-realisation record cannot), and "scaled to F2x" means an observational regression estimate, not the formal 1%-per-year model experiment; establish causation by itself (that rests on radiative physics and fingerprints such as stratospheric cooling); or fully explain the 2023-25 excess warmth: the Recent 2023-25 tab accounts for roughly half of the annual-model residual with solar cycle 25, and the remainder (~0.07 °C) is about one standard error of a 3-year mean. Read that last comparison with the qualifier added in v1.7 at Recent 2023-25!B30:B32: the asymptotic AR(1) formula gives 0.067 for that standard error, the exact AR(1) variance of a mean of three gives 0.058, so the remainder is about 1.2 SE, and the residual BEFORE the solar line is about 2.2 SE. The budget is exploratory and the solar line carries its own unstated uncertainty. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 29 | Statistics: all fits are ordinary least squares with autocorrelated residuals (lag-1 ≈ 0.5 monthly, ≈ 0.3 annual; effective n ≈ 40 annual). The monthly effective n of ≈ 290 quoted here before v1.7 came from the AR(1) factor and overstates the independent information: Newey-West out to 96 lags implies a variance inflation near 14, i.e. an effective n nearer 60 monthly (Diagnostics section D item 5). Nothing published rests on the monthly slope. AR(1)-inflated standard errors and 95% intervals are given for the two headline slopes (Annual!K17:L20, Forcing!T19:U20). Lag and τ values were chosen in-sample; Kernel!P51:P60 is only a coefficient holdout with τ fixed. The nested check is Kernel!P62:Q70: a single 1958-95 split cannot identify τ (long τ, degraded holdout), but blocked 7-fold cross-validation selects the same τ values out-of-fold and gives pooled R² 0.887 vs 0.904 in-sample. Newey-West SEs (1-6 lags) on the annual slope, 0.120-0.126, confirm the AR(1) correction. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 30 | Data vintages (Sept 2026 review): ERF from the IGCC 2025 file (1750-2025), with its 5-95% percentile files used for uncertainty propagation. Main analysis uses NOAA CPC ONI on ERSSTv5, ClimateIndicator sulfate AOD (GloSSAC v2.23 basis) and NRLTSI2. The successors (ONI on ERSSTv6, GloSSAC v2.24, NOAA Solar CDR v3) were rerun on the Sensitivity tab; no result changes materially. Monthly AOD is sulfate only; Hunga Tonga stratospheric water vapour appears only in the annual volcanic ERF on the Forcing tab and in the Recent 2023-25 budget. | 44 | Breusch-Pagan and White on the monthly three-factor residuals are marginal to significant (p about 0.03 and 0.004) but the auxiliary regressions explain only 1 to 3 per cent of the squared residuals. The large ARCH statistics turn out to be an artefact of the level autocorrelation already documented here: after filtering it out, ARCH-LM at q = 1 falls from about 42 to under 1 (p about 0.4) and Breusch-Pagan is far from significant. On the two annual models almost nothing is detected (Breusch-Pagan p = 0.28 and 0.40), the one marginal statistic being White on the CO2-proxy model at p = 0.035 on 67 points. The corrections are not interchangeable: HC3, robust to heteroskedasticity alone, raises the slope standard errors by 18 per cent (annual CO2 proxy), 4 per cent (annual ERF) and 9 per cent (monthly); the AR(1) inflation addresses serial correlation only; Newey-West covers both. On both annual slopes the AR(1)-inflated standard errors published here are the widest or within a per cent of the widest of the four measures, so no published interval changes. The monthly slope, on which no interval is published, is the one place the AR(1) factor is not the conservative choice. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| 34 | 1991 | 12 | 355.7041667 | 0.4075 | 0.3452223561 | 0.02597300929 | -0.009893436622 | 0.05330110162 | 4. Uncertainty: the naive OLS standard error is inflated by the AR(1) factor (Grok/GPT review, Sept 2026); the resulting 95% interval (~2.5 to 3.0 °C per doubling) reflects time-series error only, not forcing or dataset uncertainty. Newey-West standard errors with 1-6 lags give 0.120-0.126, so the AR(1) heuristic is adequate here. The split-sample slopes (1959-1991 vs 1992-2025) differ (~2.6 vs ~3.2) but only by ~1.3 combined adjusted SEs (K22), so the difference is suggestive, not established. The direction is what the forcing data predict: net anthropogenic forcing grew faster than CO2 alone once aerosol offset stopped growing (Forcing tab, T42:U42), which is a reason to prefer the anthropogenic-ERF regression over the CO2 proxy for any response estimate. |  |  |

But the Sun is not zero: the ~11-year cycle shows up as a small positive correlation with the leftovers of the CO2 fit, and in the multiple regression as ~0.07 °C per W/m² of TSI, i.e. a ~0.1 °C peak-to-trough cycle. That matches the published estimate, and finding it is a good sign the data and method are sound. |  |

The apparent 2.74 to ~2.66 shift is the shorter window the TSI series forces (ending 2023), not the Sun: on the same months the CO2-only slope is already 2.640 (Volcanic!N31), and Sensitivity!AB22:AC22 gives 2.662 against 2.715 on the two windows. Adding lagged ONI raises monthly R² from 0.86 to 0.89 and cuts residual scatter by ~12%; the coefficient (~0.09 °C per unit ONI) matches the published ~0.1 °C per °C of Niño 3.4. |  |  |  |
| 36 | 1/1961 | 0.07 | 0.1785553066 | 0.08 | 1361.24 | 0 | 0.1684626965 | -0.0968836027 | 0.1668836027 | 0.06303697841 | 2. The lag test peaks at 3 months, the known delay for tropical Pacific heat to spread into the global mean. Obtaining that value from the data is consistent with the known physics, though it does not by itself validate the model. |  |  |  |
| 37 | 2/1961 | 0.19 | 0.1822382629 | -0.07 | 1361.13 | 0.03 | 0.2783950727 | -0.09982293803 | 0.289822938 | 0.1960926439 | 3. The CO2 coefficient barely moves (2.73 to 2.75 °C per doubling). ONI is detrended by construction (centred 30-year base periods), so it is close to orthogonal to the CO2 trend and absorbs almost none of it. Note that this is a property of the index convention, not a finding: an ENSO index built without re-centred bases, such as RONI, does carry a trend and does take some of the signal (Open Items section A). |  |  |  |
| 38 | 3/1961 | 0.09 | 0.1860477201 | -0.07 | 1361.04 | 0.01 | 0.1679816496 | -0.08935913557 | 0.1793591356 | 0.09609264389 | 4. What is still unexplained: the largest negative residuals are Jul-Sep 1992 and Apr 1964 (Pinatubo and Agung eruptions), so volcanic aerosols are the next control. The 2023-2025 residual is positive (~+0.14 °C): the recent warmth exceeds what CO2 + El Niño predict, which is an open question in the literature (aerosol reductions from shipping-fuel rules, solar cycle 25 maximum, and possibly cloud feedback are candidates). |  |  |  |

Adding lagged stratospheric AOD raises monthly R² from 0.89 to 0.90 and the coefficient (~-2.2 °C per unit AOD) implies peak cooling of ~-0.2 °C for Agung and Pinatubo and ~-0.1 °C for El Chichón, consistent with published estimates (Pinatubo ~-0.3 °C with uncertainty). Most of the 1964 and 1992 residuals on the ENSO tab are now accounted for. |  |  |  |
| 45 | 10/1961 | 0 | 0.1713440984 | 0.08 | 0.00382 | 1361.02 | 0.0043 | 0.2186 | -0.09393830791 | 0.09393830791 | 0.1166913216 | 1961.791667 | 2. The lag test peaks at 6-8 months: a short forcing pulse takes about half a year to show in the global mean because the ocean mixed layer has to cool first. Same pattern as the 3-month ENSO lag and the solar cycle: the fitted lags are consistent with known physics. |  |  |  |

The three large eruptions all sit in the first half of the record, so stratospheric AOD does carry a small sample trend and absorbs a little of the CO2 signal, but the effect is 0.02 °C per doubling. |  |  |  |
| 47 | 12/1961 | -0.16 | 0.1791015234 | -0.32 | 0.00389 | 1360.91 | 0.00411 | 0.2225 | -0.1100525372 | -0.04994746284 | -0.02980163548 | 1961.958333 | 4. The implied transient response to volcanic forcing (~0.13 °C per W/m²) is much smaller than the ~0.4 °C per W/m² implied by the solar cycle or the ~0.8 needed for equilibrium sensitivity. That is expected: a 1-2 year pulse never gets close to equilibrium, so regressing on AOD says little about long-run sensitivity. |  |  |  |

Still unexplained: 2023-2025 residuals remain positive (~+0.15 °C). Volcanoes do not help; Hunga Tonga (2022) added stratospheric water vapour (a small warming) but little sulfate. The remaining candidates are anthropogenic: the 2020 shipping-fuel sulfur cut, declining Chinese SO2, and cloud feedback. Anthropogenic aerosol forcing is the logical next control. |  |  |  |

Each control now enters through an exponential response instead of a single lag: the temperature effect of this month's ONI or AOD is spread over the following months with weights (1-a)·a^k. This is the one-box energy-balance form used in the published regression literature (e.g. Foster & Rahmstorf 2011 use lags; Lean & Rind 2008 and the energy-budget papers use response kernels). |  |  | 34 | 0.0005310776416 | 0.00470270542 | -0.08339619995 |

Validation (revised after the Sept 2026 review): P51:P60 is a coefficient holdout only, because τ was chosen on the full record. A fully nested test is at P62:Q70. Choosing τ on 1958-95 alone by training R² picks long τ (24, 24) and the 1996-2025 holdout degrades (R² 0.61, bias -0.085 °C): a single early split cannot identify τ_ENSO and the max-R² rule over-smooths. Under blocked 7-fold cross-validation, with τ and coefficients both chosen out-of-fold, every fold selects τ_ENSO of 6-9 and most select τ_AOD of 12, and the pooled out-of-fold R² is 0.887 vs 0.904 in-sample (CO2-only: 0.838). The variance does depend on the regressors, but weakly, and the honest test is the filtered one. Breusch-Pagan on the raw monthly three-factor residuals is marginal (Koenker p around 0.03) and White is significant (p around 0.004), but an LM statistic of n times the auxiliary R-squared assumes independent errors in that auxiliary regression, and with lag-1 around 0.50 those p-values are not valid. The valid version is row 17, Breusch-Pagan on the AR(1)-filtered residuals, which finds nothing (p around 0.57). Either way the auxiliary regressions explain only 1 to 3 per cent of the variation in the squared residuals |  |  |  |  |  |

The large ARCH statistics are an artefact of the autocorrelation this workbook already documents, not evidence of volatility clustering. An AR(1) process in the levels produces autocorrelated squares, so ARCH-LM over-rejects when applied to residuals with lag-1 around 0.5. Removing that structure first (column AA, rho in AX16) collapses the result: ARCH-LM at q = 1 falls from about 42 to under 1 (p around 0.4), q = 6 from about 54 to about 10 (p around 0.14), and Breusch-Pagan on the filtered residuals is far from significant. Rows 17 to 19 are therefore the tests to read, and rows 11 to 13 are the ones that mislead. |  |  |  |  |  |

On the two annual models, which carry every published interval in this workbook, almost nothing is detected, with one exception worth naming rather than skipping. Anthropogenic-ERF model: Breusch-Pagan p = 0.28, White p = 0.73, but ARCH-LM at q = 1 is significant at p = 0.0075 (row 24). That one is a single-event effect, not the mechanism of item 2: it is driven by the 1992 and 1993 Pinatubo residuals (-0.254 and -0.185), and after AR(1) filtering it vanishes entirely (LM 0.001, p 0.97), whereas a pure AR(1) artefact at this rho would predict an LM near 1.1. CO2-proxy model, the one behind the published 2.51 to 2.98 interval: Breusch-Pagan p = 0.40, and ARCH-LM insignificant at q = 1, the only lag this tab tests for it (residual_diagnostics.py also runs q = 6 and 12, likewise insignificant). Its one marginal statistic is White at p = 0.035 on 67 points with an auxiliary R-squared of 0.10. Section B shows neither moves anything: HC3 on that slope is 0.1093 against the 0.1201 already published |  |  |  |  |  |

No published interval changes, but the three corrections are not interchangeable and should not be run together in one sentence. HC3 is robust to heteroskedasticity alone, and raises the slope standard errors by 18 per cent (annual CO2 proxy), 4 per cent (annual ERF) and 9 per cent (monthly). The AR(1) inflation addresses serial correlation only, through an effective-sample-size adjustment. Newey-West is robust to both together. On both annual rows the AR(1)-inflated standard error this workbook publishes is the widest or within a per cent of the widest of the four measures: ERF 0.0167 against 0.0125 for Newey-West at 6 lags; CO2 proxy 0.1201 against 0.1202 at 6 lags, where the widest lag choice in 1 to 6 gives 0.1260 and would move the 95 per cent interval from 2.51-2.98 to 2.50-2.99. So the heteroskedasticity found in section A is not a reason to widen any published interval. |  |  |  |  |  |

The monthly row is the exception, and the published figure understates it. At 12 lags the Newey-West standard error is 0.081, about 1.4 times the AR(1)-inflated 0.057, but it has not converged there: 0.067 at 6 lags, 0.081 at 12, 0.100 at 24, 0.112 at 36, 0.121 at 60, 0.1225 at 96, with the residual autocorrelation showing bumps near lags 12 and 24. The converged value is about 0.122, which is about 2.2 times the AR(1) figure and, tellingly, equal to the annual CO2-proxy slope standard error of 0.1201. So at monthly resolution the AR(1) factor understates the dependence by about half. No interval in this workbook rests on the monthly slope (every published interval is annual: Annual!J20:L20, Forcing!S43:U43, Sensitivity!AC46), so nothing propagates, but the monthly AR(1) figure should not be quoted as a bound, and the 'effective n of about 290 monthly' at Summary!B29 is not supported by the autocorrelation function |  |  |  |  |  |

The recent warmth is a shift in the mean, not a widening of the spread, and row 52 is the figure that shows it. Measured about its own mean the 2016-2026 subset has a standard deviation 1.14 times the all-month value (row 42), but that subset straddles a step: the 2016-2022 mean is -0.008 and the 2023-2025 mean is +0.146. Measured about those two means separately the ratio is 0.97 (row 52), so the spread is if anything slightly narrower than the record as a whole and the 1.14 is the mean shift being counted as spread. That supports treating the 2023-2025 excess as a forcing and response question, as the Recent 2023-25 tab does, rather than as a change in noise |  |  |  |  |  |

Caveats. These are in-sample diagnostics on residuals from models whose lag structure was selected in sample, and the LM tests assume the auxiliary regressions are themselves correctly specified. The subset standard deviations in section C are descriptive: the subsets were chosen because eruptions and ENSO extremes are where clustering would be expected, not by a search. Two further structural notes. The monthly CO2 regressor keeps the Mauna Loa seasonal cycle (about plus or minus 0.027 doublings), which is not a forcing; using the deseasonalised column moves the slope from 2.7274 to 2.7359 and the residual standard deviation from 0.1221 to 0.1215, so it is negligible for the slopes, but the monthly residuals retain a calendar-month structure of about 0.10 degC range that survives deseasonalisation and is the source of the lag-12 and lag-24 bumps noted in item 5. And the same record was used to select the lag structure, to run these diagnostics and to compute the 2023-2025 budget |  |  |  |  |  |

| 32 | 9/1960 | 1960.708333 | 0.17 | 0.04 | 0.07 | 0.1661185975 | 0.00397 | 0 | 0.1661185975 | 0.00397 | 0.04 | 0.1661185975 | 0.00397 | -0.2327674378 | 1989 | 0.2741666667 | 1.1875 | -1.019166667 | 1.1875 | -1.04 | 1.1875 | -1.076902519 | 2.5716 | -2.311447 | -1.019166667 | 0.06097733107 | Reading section A, revised in v1.6. RONI makes the fit worse, not better, and raises the CO2 coefficient by about 0.09 monthly and the headline annual value from 1.607 to 1.665. That shift is entirely attributable to RONI's secular trend: removing its linear trend returns the coefficient to the ONI baseline to within 0.0001 (rows 17 and 19). Two cautions about how far that goes. Detrending any regressor hands its trend variance back to log2(CO2), which is nearly linear in time, so the detrending result is close to a tautology and is not evidence about which index is right. And ONI's own flat trend is equally a product of its convention, its re-centred 30-year bases, so preferring it is an assumption that no forced change in the tropical Pacific SST gradient belongs with the ENSO term. What the record cannot do is settle that question. So this is better reported as a structural uncertainty of about +0.06 degC per doubling on the headline, roughly twice the dataset sensitivity of plus or minus 0.03 at Sensitivity!AA84, than as a closed item. On construction, RONI is the Nino 3.4 anomaly minus the tropical-mean SST anomaly, so it falls mechanically if the tropical mean warms faster than Nino 3.4, and empirically the divergence tracks the warming (row 14). Separately from all of that, the 2023-2025 residual gets LARGER under RONI, because RONI scores the 2023-24 El Nino near 1.5 against ONI's 2.0, so the recent excess is not an artefact of the ENSO index. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | -0.02 | 1960.708333 | 0.07 |

Until that revision this regression used GHG ERF alone as the warming regressor and omitted Forcing column J, the other anthropogenic terms (ozone, land use, contrails, BC on snow, stratospheric water vapour), even though the headline regressor is L = K + I + J. Column J trends 0.13 to 0.48 W/m2 and correlates 0.98 with GHG, so its effect was absorbed into g, which is why g came out at 0.467 against a headline b of 0.409. The apparent 0.10 difference between the GHG and aerosol responses was an omitted-variable artefact. With J restored the two responses are 0.409 and 0.414, a difference of -0.005 (row 45), so they are indistinguishable, which is exactly what the headline single-ERF regression assumes. What remains true, and is the real content of this section: the warming-term and aerosol series are nearly orthogonal over this record (row 35), so the regression separates them and the two estimates are almost uncorrelated; and scaling the aerosol series by s scales h by exactly 1/s while leaving h x s and the R^2 unchanged (row 50 against row 40), so the aerosol CONTRIBUTION is identified and the response per W/m2 is not, because the series magnitude is uncertain by a factor of four at AR6's 5-95%. Note also what a failure to reject does not buy: the 95% interval on g - h is -0.20 to +0.19, so the test is weak, and the right reading is that the data give no reason to prefer different responses, not that they confirm equal ones. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | -0.02 | 1962.291667 | 0.05 |

The shortwave decline cannot be entered in the residual budget as an independent forcing line, and that holds at either response rate. At the sustained rate it implies 0.53 degC, 7.7 times the remainder; at the pulse rate that Forcing!S61 argues is appropriate for short-lived forcing, and that the Recent 2023-25 tab itself uses for Hunga Tonga over this very window, it implies 0.16 degC, still 2.4 times the remainder. The pulse rate is the internally consistent one for a three-year flux change, so read row 59's second figure. The raw shortwave change is also 1.50 times the whole change in total ERF between the same two windows (row 61; against the change in the CERES net imbalance the ratio is about 2.4, and the two should not be conflated). A top-of-atmosphere flux change mixes externally forced cloud and albedo change, feedback to the warming, and internal variability, and nothing here decomposes it. What these numbers establish is that the whole SW change cannot be treated as forcing: the implied warming exceeds both the remainder and the independently estimated change in forcing, and the fitted response coefficient already contains whatever part of the SW change is feedback, so adding it would count that part twice. Consistent with that, outgoing longwave rose by about as much as absorbed shortwave over the same window while the net imbalance rose far less. The roughly 0.07 degC remains unexplained. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 0.11 | 1963.291667 | -0.07 |

| 24 | How to read this |  |  |  |  |
| 25 | 1. In the monthly model, the three forcings the literature names for 2023-25 (aerosol decline, solar maximum, Hunga Tonga water vapour), valued at this workbook's own fitted responses, sum to roughly the residual. That is stronger than "open question" and weaker than "explained": each line has its own uncertainty, and the water-vapour line spans a factor of three depending on whether the pulse or sustained response applies. The solar line now uses the actual NOAA Solar CDR v3 values for 2023-25 rather than an assumed level. |  |  |  |  |
| 26 | 2. In the annual model, aerosols and water vapour are already fitted, and ~0.13 °C remains. Solar accounts for roughly half. What is left (~0.07 °C) is about one standard error of a 3-year mean residual, so it cannot be distinguished from single-realisation noise with this record. It also cannot be ruled out as something real, e.g. the low-cloud / albedo decline reported in CERES data, which is not a separate line here because it may be the mechanism through which the aerosol change acts rather than an addition to it. |  |  |  |  |
| 27 | 3. Both residuals are relative to models fitted over the whole record, so "solar" here means the departure of the cycle-25 maximum from the average solar level in the fit, not the full cycle amplitude. Caution: refitting the solar coefficient with 2024-25 included raises it (Sensitivity tab), because those years are both solar-maximum and unusually warm; using the 1959-2023 coefficient avoids letting the years being explained shape the explanation. |  |  |  |  |
| 28 | 4. Tested on the Sensitivity tab (AA55:AH86): with HadCRUT5 in place of GISTEMP the monthly residual is +0.13 and the annual residuals +0.11 / +0.10, so what remains after solar is about 0.05 °C rather than 0.07. Berkeley Earth (to Dec 2024) gives values close to GISTEMP. Dataset choice adds roughly ±0.02-0.03 °C to the uncertainty of every line on this tab. RONI instead of ONI remains untested. |  |  |  |  |
| 30 | Added v1.7: how large is that standard error, exactly? |  |  |  |  |
| 31 |   Exact AR(1) standard error of a mean of three annual residuals | 0.05764634685  {=D18/3*SQRT(3+2*(2*Forcing!T18+Forcing!T18^2))} | E18 uses the asymptotic factor sqrt((1+rho)/(1-rho))/sqrt(3), which overstates it for n = 3 |  |  |
| 32 |   Remainder after solar (D17), in units of that standard error | 1.183243807  {=D17/D31} | about 1.2 SE, so still not distinguishable from noise |  |  |
| 33 |   Residual BEFORE the solar line (D15), in the same units | 2.187124487  {=D15/D31} | about 2.2 SE: the excess is only insignificant after a solar line whose own uncertainty is not propagated |  |  |

GloSSAC v2.24 agrees with the ClimateIndicator AOD series to r ≈ 0.99 and has the same Pinatubo peak, but a lower quiet-period background (≈0.010 vs 0.014). That makes eruptions stand out more against background, so the volcanic coefficient strengthens (≈ -2.6 vs -2.2 °C per unit AOD) and the implied Pinatubo cooling rises to ≈ -0.28 °C; R² rises by 0.001 and the CO2 slope moves by -0.02. NOAA Solar CDR v3 (NNLTSI1) sits 0.56 W/m² above NRLTSI2 on a new absolute scale (TSIS-1), with r ≈ 0.995 between the two annual series and no relative trend; the offset goes into the intercept and the solar coefficient on the common 1959-2023 window is unchanged (0.068 vs 0.067 °C per W/m²). Extending the fit to 2025 raises the coefficient to ≈ 0.09 because 2024-25 are both solar-maximum years and unusually warm years; that is the solar term absorbing part of the 2023-25 residual, not new information about the Sun, and it is why the Recent 2023-25 tab uses the 1959-2023 coefficient. The biggest ERF uncertainty (aerosol-cloud interactions, ±75%) barely moves the result. The regression responds to the change in forcing across 1959-2025, and net aerosol forcing changed little between those endpoints (-0.91 to -0.96 W/m²; it deepened through the 1980s to about -1.4 and reached -1.49 in 1991, then recovered). Scaling the aerosol series therefore changes the shape of the forcing curve, not its trend, and the fitted slope moves by only about ±0.03 °C per doubling. Ozone and CO2 matter more because their series trend. |  |  |  |  | 2007 | 0.6641666667 | 1361.169 | 0.4557562087 | 1360.604167 | 0.0997 | 0.1107 | 0.1606881172 | 0.1673459824 | 0.6608416667 | 0.6798666667 |

CO2-ERF uncertainty and F2x uncertainty are the same physical quantity. Scaling the CO2 series down makes b larger and F2x smaller, partly offsetting: a ±12% scaling of CO2 moves b × F2x by about ±7% (AC43), not zero, because CO2 is 0.7 to 2.3× of the regressor rather than all of it. Treating the two as independent (row 47, and Forcing!T43:U43) therefore overstates the width. The full Monte Carlo (row 46), which ties them together, gives 1.43-1.78 (90%), narrower than the quadrature 1.36-1.85. |  |  |  |  | 2008 | 0.5433333333 | 1361.197 | 0.4625343313 | 1360.61 | 0.0582 | 0.0337 | 0.1187052306 | 0.08978419487 | 0.5345166667 | 0.5520333333 |

Method limits: component uncertainties are sampled as independent normal scale factors on the best-estimate time series, which is how the IGCC ensemble is built for most components, but not for all. Three components have percentile ranges bounded at zero (ARI -0.469 to -0.001, BC on snow -0.000 to +0.180, stratospheric H2O -0.000 to +0.100), so a symmetric normal flips their sign in about 5 to 7 per cent of draws. Those three are small enough that the headline is unaffected (ARI's whole single-component range is 1.55 to 1.66), but the sampling does not mirror the IGCC ensemble for them. The scheme also ignores the ARI/ACI correlation and any shape uncertainty. The pointwise percentile rows (38-39) are shown because reviewers asked for them, but percentile envelopes are not ensemble members and should not be read as a fit to a plausible forcing history. The three datasets agree with GISTEMP to r ≈ 0.99 monthly and within ±0.01 °C in mean level. HadCRUT5 reproduces the GISTEMP coefficients almost exactly (CO2 slope 2.73 vs 2.73; ENSO 0.094 vs 0.093). Berkeley Earth runs warmer over time: its CO2 slope on the same months to Dec 2024 is 2.80 against 2.68 for GISTEMP (column AE), a difference of about 0.12 °C per doubling, or 0.07 on the ERF-scaled value (1.66 vs 1.59 on the same years). That is a real difference in the trend of the two records, consistent with the Berkeley record's slightly larger long-term warming, and it is inside the AR(1) interval for the slope (Forcing!T20:U20). |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | -0.2939 | -0.2523 | -0.05386528404 | -0.02003640598 |  |  |

The 2023-25 residual is the quantity most sensitive to dataset: HadCRUT5 gives +0.13 monthly and +0.11 annual (+0.10 with volcanic ERF) against GISTEMP's +0.15 / +0.14 / +0.13. HadCRUT5 warms slightly less than GISTEMP in 2023-25, mainly in the Arctic where the two datasets treat coverage differently. Berkeley is only available to Dec 2024 here, so its 2023-24 residual is not directly comparable. The Recent 2023-25 tab budget is therefore built on the higher of the two full-record values; with HadCRUT5, what remains after solar is about 0.05 °C rather than 0.07. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | -0.1871 | -0.1853 | 0.01619531978 | 0.01086728243 |  |  |

| 34 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | With AR6 values for F2x and ECS, the rise in ERF over the period predicts a rise in N of about 0.25 W/m²; CERES observes about 0.5 W/m². The excess is real and is the subject of current literature (the 2010s-2020s decline in reflected SW: cloud and sea-ice albedo, aerosol clean-up, IMO 2020). It is not evidence that the temperature regression is wrong, but it is a reason not to treat a 20-year energy-budget ECS as robust: ΔT is only ~0.36 °C and the pattern effect is unaccounted for. |  | 2002 | 8 | 2002.625 | -6.5795 | 244.577 | 93.8173 | 2012 | 6 | 15.461417 |
| 35 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | The useful confirmations are the signs and magnitudes: N is positive every year, its trend is the same order as the ERF trend, and nearly all the growth in N is in reflected SW (falling), not outgoing LW (rising, as expected from a warming surface). Any model in which forcing is not rising would need N to be flat or falling. |  | 2002 | 9 | 2002.7083 | -1.1693 | 243.163 | 94.4619 | 2012 | 9 | 15.34632 |
| 36 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | The ocean closes the loop from below, but only partly. NCEI 0-2000 m heat uptake averages about 0.65 W/m² against a CERES N of about 1.0 over the same years, a ratio near 0.66. Published budgets put ~89% of N in the whole ocean (von Schuckmann et al. 2023); the gap here is the deep ocean below 2000 m (~0.05-0.1 W/m²), the ~10% in land, ice and atmosphere, and the fact that the NCEI product runs low relative to IAP/Cheng et al. OHC has risen every year since 2005 without exception. Two honest caveats: the 2006-2024 trend in ocean uptake (~0.15 W/m² per decade) is only a third of the CERES trend in N (~0.45), and the year-to-year correlation is essentially zero. Annual N is noisy, the centred OHC difference smooths over three years, and Argo sampling error on a single year is of order 0.3 W/m², so the agreement to look for is in the multi-year means, not the annual values. Whether the recent CERES trend is fully reflected in the ocean is an open question in the literature. |  | 2002 | 10 | 2002.7917 | 2.5889 | 240.044 | 99.6375 | 2012 | 12 | 16.630146 |
| 37 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | CERES absolute accuracy is ±1-2 W/m²; the multi-year mean of N is anchored to Argo OHC by the CERES team itself (Loeb et al. 2021), so the two series are not fully independent in level. They are independent in trend and interannual variation, which is what is compared here. |  | 2002 | 11 | 2002.875 | 3.5199 | 237.885 | 106.317 | 2013 | 3 | 20.31798 |

One small difference, recorded rather than smoothed over: the aerosol range here is -1.6003 to -0.3891 against the paper's -1.58 to -0.40, 0.02 and 0.01 apart, which is what a pointwise percentile envelope gives against an ensemble quantile. | 47 | Anthropogenic waste heat (~0.04 W/m² global mean, ~1 to 1.5% of total ERF; datacenters ~0.0002 to 0.0004 W/m²) is not included in the AR6 ERF series. It co-varies with CO2 and is absorbed into the anthropogenic coefficients; its 2019 to 2025 change (~0.003 W/m², about 0.001 °C at Forcing!T14) is negligible against the 2023 to 2025 residual on the Recent 2023-25 tab. It also leaves the CERES tab's λ and ECS check effectively unchanged, since its decade-to-decade change is a few thousandths of a W/m². |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 48 | Basis: global primary energy use ~620 EJ/yr (~19 to 20 TW) spread over 5.10×10¹⁴ m². Datacenter electricity 2025: ~485 TWh (IEA, Key Questions on Energy and AI, 2026) to ~788 TWh (Energy Institute, Statistical Review of World Energy 2026, S&amp;P Global data), multiplied by ~2 to 2.5 for primary energy (power-plant conversion losses), giving ~1,000 to 2,000 TWh/yr. Comparable published estimate: Flanner, M.G. (2009), Integrating anthropogenic heat flux with global climate models, Geophys. Res. Lett. 36, L02801, doi:10.1029/2008GL036465 (verified against Crossref 2026-10-23: Flanner, M.G., single author, Geophys. Res. Lett. 36(2), article 2008GL036465, 2009). | 49 | Item 15, resolved 2026-10-23 (v1.7.10). The RONI series is now ingested directly from RONI.v5.ascii.txt with the sha256 recorded at E45, so the CHECK closes against a download rather than the HTML transcription it carried from 2026-10-22. The transcription was faithful: every one of its 917 values was the exact one-decimal rounding of the published two-decimal value under ties-toward-positive-infinity, tested against five conventions, with no transcription errors. Ninety-four of the 917 published values sit exactly on a rounding tie, so the convention mattered for about one value in ten. Recovering the second decimal changed no reported figure: the RONI headline moved 1.6650 to 1.6649 and the structural uncertainty +0.0583 to +0.0582. WARNING, and the reason E45 names the file: CPC publishes two RONI series and they are not vintages of one another. RONI.ascii.txt is the operational index adopted for official ENSO monitoring on 2026-02-01 (NWS PNS 26-05); RONI.v5.ascii.txt is the ERSSTv5 basis used here, for consistency with the ONI v5 input at item 5. Over the 917 shared seasons only 49 values (5.3 per cent) are identical, the mean absolute difference is 0.0799, the largest is 0.52 at MJJ 1952, and 43 seasons (4.7 per cent) fall on opposite sides of the plus or minus 0.5 event threshold. The v5 file also lags by three seasons, ending AMJ 2026 against JAS 2026. Anything that says only CPC RONI is now ambiguous. On permanence, treat the v5 file as unassured. PNS 26-05 says the legacy Nino 3.4 and Oceanic Nino Index files will continue to be updated and that no legacy data files or web links would change at implementation, but it names neither of those as RONI.v5.ascii.txt and does not mention that file at all; the only RONI file it points to is the operational one. Checked here on 2026-10-23: the CPC indices page lists RONI.ascii.txt and oni.ascii.txt and does not list RONI.v5.ascii.txt, which resolves and returns data but is unlinked. The sha256 at E45 and the retrieval date are therefore the record if that file moves or stops being updated. |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| 16 | v1.7.3 | 2026-10-22 | Correction | 2026-10-22 (v1.7.3): a real defect, found only because the file was opened and saved in Excel and the Excel-computed cache compared against the export. Seven formulas in Diagnostics section C passed a lone boolean array to SUMPRODUCT, for example =SUMPRODUCT(($B$9:$B$822>=2016)) at AX42. Excel does not coerce a bare boolean array to numbers, so those seven returned 0 and the eighteen cells that divide by them showed #DIV/0!; LibreOffice does coerce it, so the pasted figures, all four scripts and every Markdown export have been numerically right the whole time while the live Excel display was wrong. The seven now read SUMPRODUCT(--(...)), which both engines evaluate the same way, and nothing downstream changed. The condition dates from v1.1, when the tab was added: Diagnostics ships with no cached values, so Excel recomputed it on open and showed the errors to anyone who opened the file, while every review in the chain, including the adversarial ones, read the LibreOffice-derived Markdown and saw correct numbers. Checking one engine's output against itself is not a check. |

| 19 | v1.7.6 | 2026-10-23 | Correction | 2026-10-23 (v1.7.6): corrections to the three reference tabs added hours earlier, after an independent review. ONI against RONI had the trend direction backwards: ONI is detrended by construction through its re-centred 30-year bases and carries -0.005 degC per decade (Open Items!AB10), so it absorbs almost none of the CO2 signal, while RONI subtracts the tropical mean and carries -0.083 (AB7), and it is that trend competing with log2(CO2) which moves the headline. ENSO!M37 had said so since v1.1, and the Acronyms entry for RONI repeated the same reversal. Autocorrelation quoted 0.36 to 0.6 for the monthly models from a cell holding an annual figure; monthly runs 0.47 to 0.64 and annual 0.25 to 0.36. Four smaller errors: the ARCH collapse was cited to AW56, which covers the annual models, rather than AW55; ERSST called v6 an untested successor when Sensitivity!AA29 reports it tested and indistinguishable; Monte Carlo claimed to handle correlated inputs when AA52 says components are sampled independently and the ARI/ACI correlation ignored, its real advantage being the CO2-to-F2x tie at row 46; and one tab name was miscased. | 21 | v1.7.8 | 2026-10-23 | Documentation | 2026-10-23 (v1.7.8): terms of use stated, ahead of a public repository. Until now Sources column K recorded the terms of all sixteen inputs and the file said nothing about its own, so the default a recipient had to assume was all rights reserved, which strictly means the reviewers it was sent to could not redistribute it. Sources section F now states CC BY 4.0 on the workbook, its notes and the Markdown exports, and the MIT licence on the four scripts in section E, Creative Commons advising against CC terms for software. CC BY 4.0 rather than a NonCommercial or ShareAlike licence for three reasons: NonCommercial is deliberately undefined and would create doubt for industry readers, ShareAlike would bind anyone lifting a figure into a report, and both can collide with journal and preprint requirements for CC BY. | 23 | v1.7.10 | 2026-10-23 | Correction | 2026-10-23 (v1.7.10): RONI re-ingested from the file the workbook said did not exist. Sources item 15 recorded the series as transcribed from an HTML table because CPC published no file for it. CPC does publish one, at https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/data/indices/RONI.v5.ascii.txt, 917 rows at two decimals where the HTML table gives one. Column C of Open Items now carries those published values, 735 of its 819 rows changing in the second decimal, and the CHECK marker closes against a download with a recorded sha256 rather than a text extraction. The superseded transcription was not at fault: all 917 of its values are the exact one-decimal rounding of the published values under ties-toward-positive-infinity, with no transcription errors, which was tested against five rounding conventions. Only the premise was wrong. Recovering the second decimal moves nothing that is reported: the RONI headline goes from 1.6650 to 1.6649 and the structural uncertainty from +0.0583 to +0.0582, with the detrended variant identical to four decimals. A separate finding, not previously on any list: the two RONI files CPC publishes are different series, not different vintages of one. Over the 917 shared seasons only 5.3 per cent of values are identical, the mean absolute difference is 0.08, the largest is 0.52 at MJJ 1952, and 4.7 per cent of seasons fall on opposite sides of the plus or minus 0.5 event threshold, so the two disagree about event classification for roughly one season in twenty. RONI.ascii.txt is the operational series CPC adopted for official ENSO monitoring on 2026-02-01; RONI.v5.ascii.txt is the ERSSTv5 basis, which is the one consistent with this workbook's ONI input. Sources now names the file rather than saying CPC RONI, because that phrase has come to denote the other series. The citation at L45 was also wrong: it gave the two ERSSTv6 papers, neither of which defines the index. The index paper is L'Heureux et al. (2024), verified against Crossref. Two CHECK markers close with this revision: the RONI provenance, and the citation question at K45, which resolves as no, CPC requests no citation for RONI, on the authority of NWS PNS 26-05, which requests none and cites nothing. Two further provenance records were folded in before this build was saved, and both needed correcting first. The paper's data availability statement points to https://github.com/michellelheureux/Relative-SST/ as code computing the index from ERSSTv5, and that was offered as the authoritative tie between the file name and the v5 basis. Cloning it shows otherwise: at commit 6931301 the computing notebook is compute_relNino34_RONI_ERSSTv6.ipynb, reading ERSSTv6 from NOAA PSL, and the only ERSSTv5 in the repository rescales NMME forecasts in a different notebook. It is recorded at L45 as the reference implementation of the method, with that caveat, and not as evidence of the basis. Second, PNS 26-05's promise that legacy files keep being updated was offered as making the v5 file's survival expected. It names the legacy Nino 3.4 and Oceanic Nino Index files and never mentions RONI.v5.ascii.txt, and the CPC indices page, checked here, lists RONI.ascii.txt and oni.ascii.txt but not the v5 file, which resolves while unlinked. B49 therefore keeps the permanence caveat rather than retiring it. |
| 24 | v1.7.11 | 2026-10-23 | Correction | 2026-10-23 (v1.7.11): the three remaining pre-publication items closed, and a new one opened in the process. Every citation in section A was checked against the publisher record rather than re-read: Lenssen 2019, Coddington 2016, Huang 2017, Kovilakam 2020, Morice 2021 and Rohde and Hausfather 2020 all reproduce exactly as written, which is six of seven. The seventh was wrong. L8 cited doi:10.15138/9N0H-ZH07 for the Mauna Loa CO2 record, and DataCite gives that as 'Trends in globally-averaged CO2 determined from NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory measurements', a different product. Worse, the correct citation is two-part and the second half was missing entirely: the imported file header states that March 1958 through April 1974 was obtained by C. David Keeling of Scripps, and this workbook's series starts in March 1958, so sixteen years of its CO2 input are Scripps data that the workbook was not crediting. L8 now carries both, with Keeling et al. (1976) verified. L13's CHECK closes: the IGCC 2025 paper is Forster et al. (2026), Earth Syst. Sci. Data 18(6), 3889-3933, doi:10.5194/essd-18-3889-2026, published 11 June 2026. The NOAA Climate Data Record question closes too, on the agency's own document: UseAgreement_01B-32.pdf states that the CDR data sets are non-proprietary and publicly available with no restrictions on use, citation urged rather than required, no notification requirement, and the only carve-out is production software this workbook does not ship. Items 13 and 14 had columns J, K and L blank on both rows, not just the terms column, so the workbook used CERES EBAF and the NCEI ocean heat content series while naming no paper for either; both now carry their location, terms and citation, Loeb et al. (2018) and Levitus et al. (2012), both verified. One handed-over finding did not survive checking: the IPCC AR6 Chapter 7 title was said to need a serial comma, and the publisher record has none before 'and Climate Sensitivity', so the form already here was right; what was missing was the chapter DOI, now added. The new item is at L13 and it is not cosmetic. The ClimateIndicator README at commit 852f4f7, the commit these ERF files came from, warns that 2025 values are preliminary and based on extrapolations and estimates, not final until IGCC 2025 published. That paper appeared four days before the commit and nothing in the repository says whether the commit's output is the final assessment. That was opened and closed within this revision. Re-pulling settles nothing, because origin/main is still 852f4f7 four months on, so there is no newer commit; but the published paper settles it directly. Forster et al. give total anthropogenic ERF of 3.10 [2.35 to 3.83] W/m2 for 2025, with 2.37 from CO2 and aerosol -0.96 [-1.58 to -0.40]. The shipped files give anthro 3.1035, p05 2.3460, p95 3.8347, CO2 2.3709, aerosol -0.9618, so the best estimates and the total anthropogenic range agree exactly at the paper's precision. The README warning is stale text: git shows it entered on 2026-03-24 with the 2025-prelim merge and the README has not been touched since, while the output files were revised on 2026-05-29 and 2026-06-08, after the paper's revision round. One difference is recorded rather than smoothed over: the aerosol percentile range here is -1.6003 to -0.3891 against the paper's -1.58 to -0.40, which is a pointwise envelope against an ensemble quantile, a distinction Sensitivity!AA52 already draws. With that, nothing stands between this file and publication except the decision to publish. One correction fell out of the audit rather than a review. Open Items!AA66 said every month-to-month RONI minus ONI difference was within 0.76, and at two decimals one pair reaches 0.78: January 1992, RONI 2.32 against ONI 1.54. The old bound was an artifact of the rounding, since the one-decimal RONI read 2.3 there and 2.3 minus 1.54 is exactly 0.76. AA66 is rewritten: it had also still described the HTML transcription, asserted that CPC publishes no ascii file, and ended with a caveat about not being cryptographically verified, all three superseded by the re-ingestion two revisions earlier. The correlation, the decade-by-decade divergence and the event positions all still hold. |

| 49 | NNLTSI1 | NASA NOAA LASP Total Solar Irradiance, model version 1. The solar variability model behind NOAA Solar CDR v3. The naming is confusing and deliberately so on NOAA's part: the CDR release is version 3 while the model it uses is version 1, the numbering having been restarted to distinguish these models from their original Naval Research Laboratory formulation. So NNLTSI1 and NRLTSI2 are different models, not a typo for one another, and the workbook is right to treat them as two series. | Recent 2023-25!E9 |

| 52 | O3 | Ozone. One of the other anthropogenic forcing terms. | Forcing!J1 |
| 53 | OHC | Ocean heat content. Here the 0-2000 m layer, whose rate of change should account for most of the top-of-atmosphere imbalance. | CERES!A2 |
| 54 | OLS | Ordinary least squares. The unadjusted regression, whose standard errors this workbook treats as too small. | Annual!J17 |

| 58 | RMSE | Root mean square error. Used to compare models fold by fold in the cross-validation. | Summary!B41 |
| 59 | RONI | Relative Oceanic Nino Index. Nino 3.4 measured against the tropical-mean SST anomaly, which means it falls as the wider tropics warm faster than Nino 3.4 and so carries a -0.083 degC per decade trend of its own, against -0.005 for ONI. That trend competes with log2(CO2), which is why substituting RONI moves the headline. Tested in v1.4 and carried as a structural uncertainty, not adopted. See the Glossary entry for the full comparison. | ENSO!M37 |
| 60 | AI | Artificial intelligence. Appears only in the title of the IEA report cited in the datacentre waste-heat note, which is documentation and feeds no cell. | Sources!B48 |

| 62 | BAMS | Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society. Appears inside the DOI of the Coddington et al. (2016) solar irradiance paper. | Sources!L9 |
| 63 | DJF, MAM, JJA, SON | December-January-February, March-April-May, June-July-August, September-October-November. The four three-month seasons, as GISTEMP column headers. None of them feeds the analysis, which uses monthly and annual values. | GLB.Ts+dSST (4)!P2 |
| 64 | EJ | Exajoule, 10^18 joules. Used for global primary energy in the waste-heat note. | Sources!B48 |
| 65 | ESRL | Earth System Research Laboratories, NOAA. The former name of the division that is now GML, preserved in the header text of the downloaded CO2 file. | co2_annmean_mlo!A31 |
| 66 | FAQ | Frequently asked questions. The GISTEMP FAQ page is cited as a source document. | Sources!E19 |
| 67 | GPT | The OpenAI model family, named where a review note records which models raised a point. | Annual!J34 |
| 68 | HTML | HyperText Markup Language. Relevant because CPC publishes RONI only as an HTML table with no plain-text file, which is why Sources item 15 carries a CHECK marker. | Open Items!AA66 |
| 69 | IAP | Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Its ocean heat content product runs higher than the NCEI one used here, which the CERES tab notes as part of the gap in the energy budget. | CERES!N36 |
| 70 | IEA | International Energy Agency. Source of the datacentre electricity figure in the waste-heat note. | Sources!B48 |
| 71 | JCLI | Journal of Climate. Appears inside the DOI of the Huang et al. (2017) ERSST paper. | Sources!L11 |
| 72 | LaRC | Langley Research Center, NASA. Hosts the CERES data archive. | Sources!D43 |
| 73 | NASA | National Aeronautics and Space Administration. Source of GISTEMP, the GISS stratospheric aerosol reduction and the CERES products. | Analysis!H16 |
| 74 | NOAA20 | The NOAA-20 satellite, one of the three platforms named in the CERES EBAF data DOI. | Sources!D43 |
| 75 | OPeNDAP | Open-source Project for a Network Data Access Protocol. The service through which the global-mean CERES variables were retrieved rather than downloading the whole file. | Sources!E43 |
| 76 | TERRA | NASA's Terra satellite, one of the three platforms named in the CERES EBAF data DOI. | Sources!D43 |
| 77 | TSIS-1 | Total and Spectral Solar Irradiance Sensor 1. Its measurements define the newer absolute scale on which NOAA Solar CDR v3 sits 0.56 W/m2 above NRLTSI2; the offset goes into the intercept and changes no coefficient. | Sensitivity!AA31 |
| 78 | TW, TWh | Terawatt and terawatt-hour, 10^12 watts and 10^12 watt-hours. Units in the waste-heat note. | Sources!B48 |
| 79 | URL | Uniform Resource Locator. A column heading on the Sources tab. | Sources!D6 |
| 80 | US | United States. In the public-domain rights statement for the federal datasets. | Sources!K7 |
| 81 | delta, written as a Greek capital | Change in, or difference between. Used as delta-R-squared for a change in fit and delta-T for a temperature change. | Forcing!S50 |
| 82 | lambda, written as a Greek letter | The climate feedback parameter, W/m2 per degC, in the energy-balance relation N is approximately F minus lambda times delta-T. Computed, not regressed, in the CERES consistency check: N17 gives the lambda implied by the assumed ECS, F2x divided by ECS, and N20 the lambda implied by the observations, (delta-F minus delta-N) divided by delta-T. | CERES!A2 |

| 91 | SW | Shortwave. Incoming or reflected solar radiation; the CERES reflected shortwave decline is the section C candidate. | CERES!A2 |

| 94 | TSI | Total solar irradiance, W/m2. The solar input series. | Solar!D1 |

## Sheet: Glossary

Excel range A1:C41: 41 rows x 3 columns; 3 columns contain data; 0 formula cells, of which 0 belong to 0 column fills listed below.

### Cells (header row: Excel row 1)

| row | A: Glossary | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Statistical and climate terms in the sense this workbook uses them, which is not always the textbook sense: where the workbook restricts a term or warns against a reading, the entry says so. Includes this file's four local conventions (blue cells, yellow cells, the CHECK marker, and why the headline figure is not a TCR) and two traps worth knowing before editing any formula here. Every cell reference in column C was checked to resolve before this tab was written. Expansions of abbreviations are on the Acronyms tab. |  |  |
| 4 | Term | What it means in this workbook | Where to look |
| 5 | Anomaly | A temperature expressed as a departure from a baseline average rather than as an absolute. GISTEMP anomalies here are relative to 1951-1980. Regressing anomalies removes the need to model absolute temperature. | Summary!B3; GLB.Ts+dSST (4) |
| 6 | Effective radiative forcing (ERF) | The net change in energy reaching the climate system from an imposed change, in W/m2, after fast atmospheric adjustments but before the surface warms. The anthropogenic ERF series is the regressor behind the headline figure. | Forcing!L; Sources section A |
| 7 | F2x and 'per doubling' | F2x is the ERF of doubling CO2, 3.93 W/m2. A regression slope in degrees C per W/m2 multiplied by F2x gives degrees C per doubling, which is why the headline is quoted that way. | Forcing!T14 and T17; Summary!B6 |
| 8 | Why the headline is not a TCR | A TCR is defined by a specific experiment, CO2 rising 1 percent a year with everything else held fixed. This figure is a regression on observed historical forcing, which includes aerosols, volcanoes and solar, and over a period with its own forcing history. Numerical overlap with the AR6 TCR range is a comparison, not a validation. | Summary!B6 and B8 |
| 9 | Equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) | Warming from doubled CO2 after the system has fully adjusted, which takes centuries. Larger than a TCR. Used here only as an assumed value in the CERES energy-balance check. | CERES!N16 |
| 10 | Residual | What the regression does not explain: observed minus fitted. Most of the diagnostic work in this workbook is about the structure of the residuals rather than the fit. | Diagnostics; Recent 2023-25 |
| 11 | Detrended correlation | Correlation after removing a straight-line time trend from both series, so only the year-to-year wiggles are compared. It answers whether the two move together beyond a shared trend; it does not identify causation or control for ENSO. | Summary!F6 and F8 |
| 12 | Collinearity | Two regressors moving so closely together that the data cannot say which is responsible. CO2 is collinear with total human forcing, which is why the workbook does not claim to separate them. | Summary!D8 |
| 13 | Identification | Whether the data can pin down a particular quantity at all, as distinct from estimating it imprecisely. The aerosol contribution is identified here; the aerosol response per W/m2 is not, because the series magnitude is an external input. | Open Items!AA51 |
| 14 | Omitted-variable bias | A coefficient absorbing the effect of a correlated regressor that was left out. This is exactly the defect v1.6 found: the split regression omitted the other anthropogenic terms, inflating the GHG response from 0.409 to 0.467. | Summary!C24; Open Items!AA51 |
| 15 | Autocorrelation and AR(1) | Successive residuals resembling each other, so each observation carries less independent information than a count of observations suggests. The monthly models run 0.47 to 0.64 at lag 1 (Kernel!P20 0.473, Volcanic!N21 0.503, ENSO!N20 0.547, ENSO!N8 0.644). The annual models run lower, 0.25 to 0.36 (Annual!K7 0.254, Open Items!AB42 0.356, Forcing!T18 0.357), and those are the ones behind every published interval. | Annual!K7; Forcing!T18; Kernel!P20; ENSO!N8 |
| 16 | AR(1)-filtered residual | The residual series with its own one-step persistence removed, u(t) = e(t) minus rho times e(t-1). Tests run on the filtered series separate real variance clustering from an artefact of autocorrelation. Doing this is what showed the apparent ARCH violation was spurious: ARCH-LM at q = 1 falls from about 42 to under 1, in the workbook's own words at Diagnostics!AW55. | Diagnostics!AA1 and AW55 |
| 17 | AR(1)-inflated standard error | A standard error widened for autocorrelation using the lag-1 coefficient. The headline intervals use this rather than the naive OLS error. | Annual!K17:L20; Forcing!T19:U20 |
| 18 | Heteroskedasticity | Residual variance that changes across the record instead of staying constant. Present here but mild: the auxiliary regressions explain only 1 to 3 percent of the squared residuals. | Summary!B43 and B44 |
| 19 | Breusch-Pagan test, and the Koenker variant | A test for heteroskedasticity, regressing squared residuals on the regressors. The Koenker version is studentized, making it robust when the residuals are not normal; both are reported because they can disagree. | Diagnostics!AW8 |
| 20 | White test | A heteroskedasticity test that also includes squares and cross-products of the regressors, so it catches variance that depends on them non-linearly. | Diagnostics; Summary!B44 |
| 21 | Newey-West | A standard error robust to both heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation out to a chosen lag. Sensitive to that choice, which is why the workbook reports a bandwidth sequence rather than one number. | Summary!B29; Diagnostics!AW58 |
| 22 | HC3 | A heteroskedasticity-robust standard error with a small-sample correction. It does not correct for autocorrelation, so it is not interchangeable with the AR(1) inflation or with Newey-West. | Summary!B44; Diagnostics!AX31:BA33 |
| 23 | Blocked k-fold cross-validation | Splitting a time series into contiguous blocks, fitting on all but one and scoring on the one held out, so that neighbouring months do not appear on both sides. Here 7 folds on calendar decades, with both the time constants and the coefficients chosen out-of-fold. | Kernel!O62:Q70; Summary!B36:F41 |
| 24 | Out-of-fold | Chosen or scored using only data outside the fold being evaluated. Choosing the time constants in-sample and only scoring out-of-sample would understate the error, which is why the workbook states that both are chosen out-of-fold. | Summary!C23; Kernel!O67 |
| 25 | One-box exponential response, and tau | Replacing an instantaneous lag with a decaying memory of past forcing: y(t) = a*y(t-1) + (1-a)*x(t), with a = exp(-1/tau). Tau is the response time in months, about 6 for ENSO and 12 for aerosol. | Kernel; Summary!C23 |
| 26 | Lag | Using a regressor from some months earlier, since the temperature response is not instantaneous. ONI enters at a three-month lag. | ENSO; Summary!B17 |
| 27 | Pooled R-squared | The coefficient of determination computed across all held-out folds together rather than averaged per fold, so long and short folds are weighted by their size. | Kernel!P66 and P68 |
| 28 | Bias, as used on the Kernel tab | The mean of the out-of-fold prediction errors, in degrees C. Near zero means the model is not systematically high or low; it says nothing about the size of the errors, which is what RMSE reports. | Kernel!Q66; Summary!E37 |
| 29 | Quadrature | Combining independent uncertainties as the square root of the sum of their squares. The workbook flags that its quadrature row double-counts, because CO2-ERF and F2x uncertainty are the same physical quantity, and prefers the tied Monte Carlo. | Forcing!S65; Sensitivity!AA51 |
| 30 | Monte Carlo | Propagating uncertainty by drawing random values for every uncertain input many times, 20,000 here, and reading the spread of the results. Its one advantage over quadrature in this workbook is specific: the full run at Sensitivity row 46 scales F2x by the same draw as the CO2 ERF, because they are the same physical quantity, which quadrature cannot do and which narrows the 90 percent interval to 1.43-1.78 against the quadrature 1.36-1.85. It is not a general correlation fix. Sensitivity!AA52 states that the components are otherwise sampled as independent normal scale factors, and that the scheme ignores the ARI/ACI correlation and any shape uncertainty. | Sensitivity!AC46 and AA51:AA52 |
| 31 | p05 and p95 | The 5th and 95th percentiles, the bounds of a 5-95% range. AR6 reports forcing uncertainty this way, and the ERF input files come as best, p05 and p95 series. | Sensitivity!AA42; erf_inputs |
| 32 | p-value | The probability of a test statistic at least this extreme if the hypothesis being tested were true. Small means the data are surprising under that hypothesis, not that the effect is large. | Diagnostics!AZ6 |
| 33 | Stratospheric AOD | Volcanic aerosol loading high in the atmosphere, the cooling term after large eruptions. Unitless; about 0.11 at the Pinatubo peak. | Volcanic; Summary!B17 |
| 34 | ONI against RONI | ONI is Nino 3.4 temperature against centred 30-year base periods, re-centred every five years, so it is detrended by construction and carries essentially no trend over this record, -0.005 degC per decade. It is therefore close to orthogonal to the CO2 trend and absorbs almost none of it. RONI subtracts the tropical-mean SST anomaly, so it falls as the wider tropics warm faster than Nino 3.4, carrying -0.083 degC per decade, and that downward trend competes with log2(CO2). This is why substituting RONI raises the headline from 1.607 to 1.665 while making the fit worse, and why it is carried as a plus 0.06 structural uncertainty rather than adopted. ENSO!M37 stresses that the difference is a property of the index convention, not a finding about ENSO itself. | Open Items!AB7 and AB10; ENSO!M37 |
| 35 | Top-of-atmosphere imbalance | Incoming solar minus reflected shortwave minus outgoing longwave, in W/m2: the net rate at which the planet is gaining energy. Should mostly appear as rising ocean heat content. | CERES!A1 and A2 |
| 36 | Albedo | The fraction of incoming sunlight reflected back to space; a decline means more absorbed energy. The workbook does NOT reject the CERES reflected-shortwave decline as a contributor to the 2023-25 remainder. What Open Items section C establishes is narrower: the whole shortwave change cannot be entered in the residual budget as an independent forcing line, because at either response rate the warming it implies exceeds the remainder (0.53 degC sustained, 7.7 times; 0.16 degC pulse, 2.4 times) and because the fitted response coefficient already contains whatever part of the change is feedback, so adding it would count that part twice. Recent 2023-25!B26 adds that the albedo decline may be the mechanism through which the aerosol change acts rather than an addition to it. The roughly 0.07 degC remains unexplained, not explained away. | Open Items!AA63; Recent 2023-25!B26 |
| 37 | Blue cells | Workbook convention: a value computed outside Excel and pasted in. The four scripts responsible are listed in Sources section E. Blue does not survive into the Markdown export, so use Sources!B50:F55 to tell which cells these are. | Sources!B56 |
| 38 | Yellow cells | Workbook convention: a hand-maintained input, to be edited deliberately rather than recalculated. | Sources; Open Items!AB30 |
| 39 | CHECK marker | Workbook convention: a statement drafted from memory or from a source that could not be captured as a file, to be verified against the publisher record before release. Carried deliberately rather than deleted, so the gap stays visible. | Sources!B49 and item 15 |
| 40 | LINEST, and its coefficient order | The Excel array function behind the regressions. It returns coefficients in reverse order of the regressor columns, which is a standing trap when reading or editing these formulas, and it needs contiguous columns, which is why the Forcing tab repeats regressor blocks. | Annual; Forcing!S20 |
| 41 | Boolean coercion in SUMPRODUCT | A gotcha worth knowing before editing this file. SUMPRODUCT over a lone comparison, such as SUMPRODUCT((range>=2016)), returns 0 in Excel, which does not convert TRUE and FALSE to 1 and 0 for a single array, while LibreOffice does. Write SUMPRODUCT(--(range>=2016)) instead. Seven formulas on the Diagnostics tab had this defect from v1.1 to v1.7.2. | Change log, v1.7.3; Diagnostics section C |
